pr_title: JSON: Add support for Int128, UInt128 and Half
pr_body:
~~...and add Number support for `Utf8JsonReader.CopyString(...)`.~~
EDIT: Instead of changing CopyString to accept numbers, we will just enable it on an internal helper since we could regret the decission.

Fixes https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/87994

> For formating infinites we were writing them as ∞ and -∞, specifying CultureInfo.InvariantCulture fixed it.

What configuration is being used when the corresponding values for `double` and `float` are being used?

> For parsing NaN and infinites, Half.TryParse was more lax than the current S.T.Json policy and accepted them with any casing i.e: InFiNiTy could be parsed correctly; I fixed it by SequenceEquals the exact bytes we want when the TryParse method returned NaN, PositiveInfinity or NegativeInfinity.

Is this an issue though? Citing Postel's law and whatnot perhaps there is a case to be made for tolerating case insensitive identifiers. I'd be surprised if the `Half.TryParse` behavior is uninentional so perhaps it's there to address valid representations? Perhaps it's an indication that we should also make the `double` and `float` parsing logic case insensitive as well. cc @tannergooding

> What configuration is being used when the corresponding values for double and float are being used?

InvariantCulture as well, that's the default for Utf8Formatter.TryFormat:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/f7ad7265b222bede49ff93b341d81b61bd898122/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Buffers/Text/Utf8Formatter/FormattingHelpers.cs#L19
`formatText` is also equivalent to what we use for the new Converters.

> Is this an issue though?

I think it is currently an issue since it differs from the current strictness used on `double` and `float`. For consistency I suggest we follow the current convention, we should however evaluate changing it in a separate issue/thread.

issue_context.title: Extend `Utf8JsonReader.CopyString` to also accept `JsonTokenType.Number` values
issue_context.body: The current implementation of the `Utf8JsonReader.CopyString` methods only accepts JSON string tokens, that is `JsonTokenType.PropertyName` and `JsonTokenType.String`. When implementing JsonConverters for large numeric types such as `BigInteger` (https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/60780) or `Int128`/`UInt128` (https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/73500) extending the method to also handle JSON number tokens would greatly simplify getting allocation-free views of underlying JSON number encodings.

Issue Details
The current implementation of the `Utf8JsonReader.CopyString` methods only accepts JSON string tokens, that is `JsonTokenType.PropertyName` and `JsonTokenType.String`. When implementing JsonConverters for large numeric types such as `BigInteger` (https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/60780) or `Int128`/`UInt128` (https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/73500) extending the method to also handle JSON number tokens would greatly simplify getting allocation-free views of the JSON numbers.
Author: eiriktsarpalis
Assignees: -
Labels: `area-System.Text.Json`
Milestone: -

Following the discussion in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/88962#discussion_r1264957076 we have concluded that even though the functionality is useful, there is something offputting about a method called `CopyString` working with number tokens (even though JSON numbers are technically still encoded as arbitrarily long UTF-8 strings). We should consult with the API review board first, considering potential alternative method names such as `CopyValue`.

review_comments: Per @GrabYourPitchforks feedback could you add a test case that uses leading zeros?

This might be a better place to add the test case since it tests all numeric types we support:
https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/43fe8a8fc7642a1268e80b0433aebb92b049ee09/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/tests/Common/NumberHandlingTests.cs#L1044C28-L1052
Do we have any tests checking what happens when you try to deserialize a JSON number equalling `Int128.MaxValue + 1` and `Int128.MinValue - 1`?

Not exactly, but I added the following data which is making numbers that overflow:

https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/b4b569e881ab7ca04bac6969ca97f253feb0b68e/src/libraries/System.Text.Json/tests/Common/JsonNumberTestData.cs#L262-L267
We would need some kind of testing that validates handling of payloads with unsupported JSON numbers such as numbers exceeding `Int128.MaxValue` and floating point numbers.

Clarifying a bit more what I meant in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/88962/files#r1266760827, I think `TryParse` could be made to only accept a `ROS<byte>` argument and only transcode to char inside the method if `!NET8_0_OR_GREATER`.
Nit: the size of this method body seems too tiny to warrant extracting to a separate helper.

If I'm understanding this correctly, Trying to deserialize `{ "number" : NaN }` will be successful whereas `{ "number" : naN }` will fail.

However both cases are invalid JSON since non-numeric identifiers can only be contained in JSON strings.

Given that this method will get called in cases where you have `JsonTokenType.Number`, it should always reject non-numeric identifiers.
Ah right, so that case would be guarded by `Utf8JsonReader`.

> Given that this method will get called in cases where you have JsonTokenType.Number

It can actually be called when TokenType is JsonTokenType.String or JsonTokenType.PropertyName too when `ReadCore` is called from `ReadAsPropertyNameCore` or `ReadNumberWithCustomHandling`.
Nit: are you looking to avoid creating values like `NaN` and infinity here? If not just generating a random pair of bytes and passing them to BitConverter.ToHalf might be simpler.
Nevermind, I just realised you're following existing convention for other types.

> are you looking to avoid creating values like NaN and infinity here?

Yes, that was the reason why I did this method after trying with BitConverter and the random pair of bytes.
Nit: could this be a theory?
Yes it could, but this is pattern used by the nearby tests in this file.
